533.title: Stop being whirled around
533.hook: don't let outside things distract you; make time to learn something good (Meditations 2.7)
533.howItsDone: Readers who take this entry to heart often set a single aim for the day and cut one habitual distraction, using the time to study something worthwhile.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was the thirst for books: throw away the thirst, not the books. Your line was enough reading.

Eleven browser tabs. A half-written email. A notification, then another. You check the news, then the weather, then the news again, in case it changed in the last four minutes. A day like that can leave a person worn out by evening, with nothing finished to show for it. Book two has a word for that state, and it's a physical one: whirled around. Spun, like a top, or a leaf in a gust of wind.
screen: `ELEVEN TABS, NO PROGRESS.` → `A LEAF IN A GUST.` → `STOP BEING WHIRLED AROUND.`

segments.voice: First, the question. Section seven opens: do the things outside you distract you? Marcus was running an empire at war. If anyone had a reason to be distracted, it was him. Second, the cure. In Long's translation: "Give thyself time to learn something new and good, and cease to be whirled around." The cure isn't, empty your mind. It's, give yourself something good to learn. A mind with nothing to hold onto spins. A mind with something worth learning has a center. Third, the second mistake. Then Marcus catches himself, because there's a trap on the other side. Some people, he says, wear themselves out with activity, and yet have no aim to which they direct every movement and every thought. Busy, but still spinning. Being whirled around by outside things is one mistake; whirling yourself around with aimless busyness is the other. Both look like motion. Neither goes anywhere. Fourth, the aim. What Marcus wants is a center: one aim that every movement points toward. Here he doesn't say what his own aim was. It doesn't have to be grand. A good day, a kind word, a piece of work done well. The spinning slows when there's something in the middle. Not all motion has to stop. Just one spinning thing, one tab, one loop of checking, and in the time you get back, one good thing learned.

segments.voice: Let the day's spinning come to mind, the checking, the switching, the half-done things, and watch them circle like leaves in wind without fighting them. Then find the center, one aim for today, simple and real, and let your breath settle around it.
Stop being whirled around. Marcus's cure for distraction: learn something new and good, and give every movement an aim, so busyness isn't just more spinning. Today's word.
Your line: stop spinning. Something good in the middle slows the whirl. That's day five hundred thirty-three.

534.title: Attend to your own soul
534.hook: no one is unhappy for ignoring another's mind, only their own (Meditations 2.8)
534.howItsDone: Some people practicing Stoicism do brief check-ins during the day, noticing their own impressions and reactions instead of trying to decode what others are thinking.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was stop being whirled around, by outside things or by aimless busyness. Your line was stop spinning.

A colleague says fine in the meeting, and nothing else. Not fine, let's do it. Just fine, and a look at the table. What did that mean? Is he annoyed? Was it something said last week? A question like that can follow a person home and sit with them at dinner. In book two, Marcus makes a blunt observation about where that attention would be better spent.
screen: `FINE. AND A LOOK AT THE TABLE.` → `READING OTHER PEOPLE'S MINDS.` → `ATTEND TO YOUR OWN SOUL.`

segments.voice: First, the line. Section eight is two sentences. Hardly anyone, Marcus says, has been seen to be unhappy because they didn't notice what was going on in someone else's mind. But people who don't follow the movements of their own minds are bound to be unhappy. Second, the honest word. He doesn't say never. He says hardly anyone, or seldom. Sometimes misreading someone does cost something, and Marcus isn't pretending otherwise. He's pointing at which kind of attention pays. Third, the movements of the mind. For the Stoics, the mind is always moving. An impression arrives: he's annoyed with me. Then comes a moment when you agree to it, or don't. Then an impulse: send a worried text, go cold, rehearse an argument. Catching the impression before you agree to it is the heart of the practice. Epictetus said it in the handbook that opened this year: test the impression first. Marcus writes the same lesson to himself. Fourth, where to point the flashlight. You can't see into his mind, however long you replay the word fine. You can see into your own: the story you're telling, the fear under it, the reaction you're about to have. That's the one mind you can actually tend. This isn't selfishness. Elsewhere in this same book, Marcus says people were made to work together, like hands or feet. Attending to your own soul is what makes you safe to be around.

535.title: Ready to leave
535.hook: act, speak and think as one who could leave life at any moment (Meditations 2.11)
535.howItsDone: Some people who practice Stoicism use the thought of death as a prompt not to postpone what matters, such as apologies, thanks and time with people they love.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was attend to your own soul, the flashlight turned inward. Your line was mind my own mind.

Some people who travel for work keep a bag half packed. Toothbrush, charger, a clean shirt. When the call comes, they can be out the door in ten minutes, without panic, because nothing important is left undone. In book two, Marcus writes himself a note about living like that. Not about wanting to go. About being the kind of person who could, without leaving a mess of unsaid things behind.
screen: `A BAG HALF PACKED.` → `NOTHING IMPORTANT LEFT UNDONE.` → `READY TO LEAVE.`

segments.voice: First, the instruction. Section eleven begins: since you could leave life at any moment, let that shape every action, every word and every thought. It's not a threat. It's an editing rule: if this might be the last thing I do, is this how I want to do it? Second, the reasoning. Marcus thinks out loud about what leaving means. If there are gods, he says, departing isn't something to fear, because they wouldn't bring you into harm. If there were no gods, or they didn't care, why would he want to live in a world empty of them? Then he says plainly what he believes: they do exist, and they do care. People today read that passage from many places: some share his faith, some don't, some aren't sure. All of them can notice that he reasoned his way to calm, not away from the question. Third, what isn't the point. Life and death, praise and blame, pain and pleasure, money and its lack, he says, happen to good and bad people alike, so they can't be what makes a life good or bad. What makes it good is how you live it. Fourth, ready. Ready doesn't mean waiting to go, or wanting to. It means not leaving the important things for later: the apology, the thank you, the I love you you assume they know. A traveler with a half-packed bag isn't hoping to leave. They're just free to live without dread. The entry points toward a fuller life, not a shorter one.

536.title: How fast things vanish
536.hook: how quickly all things disappear, bodies and memories alike (Meditations 2.12)
536.howItsDone: Some people practicing Stoicism reflect regularly on impermanence, letting it loosen the grip of status and pleasure and sharpen their attention to the present.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was editing rule, the bag half packed. Your line was ready.

A corner store becomes a phone shop. A teacher retires and moves away. The song everyone hummed one summer stops being played. Far enough back in an old photo album, there are faces nobody in the family can name. It happens so gradually that it only shows when someone looks back. In section twelve, Marcus looks back, and looks hard, and starts with a sentence that's almost a sigh.
screen: `THE CORNER STORE IS GONE.` → `FACES NOBODY CAN NAME.` → `HOW FAST THINGS VANISH.`

segments.voice: First, two kinds of vanishing. How quickly everything disappears, Marcus says: bodies, out of the world, and then the memory of them, out of time. First the person goes. Then, more slowly, the remembering goes. Second, what dazzles. Then he looks at the things that pull hardest: things that tempt with pleasure, things that frighten with pain, things people brag about. How cheap they are, he says, how perishable, how quickly gone. It's the same trick this path met with the emperor's purple robe: looking at something until its glamour wears off. Third, death itself. Looked at alone, he says, stripped of all the imaginings piled onto it, dying is simply a work of nature. And to be terrified of a work of nature is, in his words, to be like a child. He doesn't mean grief is childish. He means the dread added on top of the plain fact. Fourth, what's near. The entry ends by pointing at something to look into, not an answer: how a human being comes near to God, by what part of himself, and when. He doesn't name the part here; a few days ago you met the one he calls the ruling part. Readers on other paths will name it differently, or not at all. But the turn is worth noticing. After everything that vanishes, he points at what's closest. Not to escape the vanishing. To stand in it, steadily, and say: so quickly. And then, still, to live today.

537.title: No prying
537.hook: nothing is more wretched than going round prying into others' souls (Meditations 2.13)
537.howItsDone: Readers who take this entry to heart often cut back on gossip and checking up on others, and turn that attention to their own character instead.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was how fast things vanish: bodies, and then their memory. Your line was so quickly.

It's eleven at night, and you're four years deep into the vacation photos of someone you don't even like. Or you're piecing together, from a coworker's tone and a calendar invite, exactly what's going on between those two. Nobody asked you to. It's not useful. It doesn't even feel good. And yet it's oddly hard to stop. A few days ago Marcus said to watch your own mind. Today he goes further, and he doesn't soften it.
screen: `FOUR YEARS INTO SOMEONE'S PHOTOS.` → `NOBODY ASKED YOU TO.` → `NO PRYING.`

segments.voice: First, the strong word. Nothing is more wretched, Marcus says, than a person who goes round and round everything, digging into the things beneath the earth, as the poet says, and trying to guess what's in the minds of the people around them. Wretched is a big word, and he means it. The prying mind is busy, restless and never full. Second, the poet. The phrase about the things beneath the earth comes from the Greek poet Pindar. Plato once borrowed it to describe a philosopher whose mind ranges over everything. Marcus turns it around: that endless searching, pointed at other people's business, is a misery, not a virtue. Third, what's enough. It's enough, he says, to attend to the guiding spirit within you, and to serve it sincerely, keeping it clean of turmoil, of carelessness, and of resentment toward gods and people. One inner life to look after is a full-time job. Fourth, how to see others. When you do look at people, Marcus says, look with affection, because they're your kin. Sometimes, even, with a kind of pity, when they don't know good from bad, which he calls a blindness no smaller than not telling black from white. Notice the order. Not suspicion, not curiosity, not judgment. Affection first. Pity, when it's called for. Prying has no place in that list. Not my business isn't coldness. It's giving people the privacy you'd want, and giving yourself back the evening.

538.title: The soul's self-harm
538.hook: the soul harms itself most when it turns against others in anger (Meditations 2.16)
538.howItsDone: Some people practicing Stoicism treat anger and resentment as harms to their own character first, and work to loosen grudges for that reason.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was no prying, and affection instead. Your line was not my business.

There's an old saying, often repeated and of uncertain origin, that holding a grudge is like drinking poison and waiting for the other person to get sick. Marcus never heard it, but his notebook circles the same idea. In section sixteen he lists the ways a soul wounds itself, and one of them is anger. A word first: Marcus means this as a picture of what anger and falseness do inside us. If the phrase self-harm touches something painful in your own life, please reach out to someone you trust today. In the US, call or text 988, any hour; elsewhere, local emergency help.
screen: `DRINKING THE POISON YOURSELF.` → `A LIST OF INNER WOUNDS.` → `IF IT'S HEAVY: 988, OR LOCAL HELP.` → `THE SOUL'S SELF-HARM.`

segments.voice: First, the claim. The soul does violence to itself, Marcus says, and he names five ways. The striking thing is the direction. Harm usually means something done to you. Marcus is interested in the harm done from the inside. Second, a growth on the world. The first way is when the soul becomes, in his image, like a swelling or a tumor on the universe: when it rages against whatever happens, as if it could pull away from the whole of nature it belongs to. Third, turning against others. The second way: when the soul turns away from another person, or moves against them meaning to hurt them, the way angry people do. Marcus's point is that anger at someone else wounds the one who carries it. People were made, he said earlier in this book, to work together, like two hands. A hand that strikes the other hand hurts the body it belongs to. Fourth, masks and aimlessness. The other ways: when the soul is overpowered by pleasure or pain; when it plays a part, saying or doing anything false; and when it acts with no aim at all, carelessly, without thinking. All five are harms done from inside. And that's practical: if the harm comes from inside, so can the repair. A grudge softened by one degree is one less wound.

539.title: A stranger's sojourn
539.hook: life is a war and a traveler's stay; what can guide us? philosophy (Meditations 2.17)
539.howItsDone: Some readers of Marcus treat life as a stay in borrowed rooms, and keep a guide, philosophical or religious, that they return to each day.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was tumor: a grudge hurts the one who holds it. Your line was don't harm myself. Today closes a week, and a book.

How do you get through a life that won't hold still? Marcus Aurelius ends his second book by piling up pictures of how short and slippery it is. A point. A river. A dream, and smoke. It reads like one long breath out. Then, at the bottom of the pile, he asks a single question: what can guide a person through all this? Today: a stranger's sojourn.
screen: `A POINT, A RIVER, SMOKE.` → `WHAT CAN GUIDE?` → `A STRANGER'S SOJOURN.`

segments.voice: Section seventeen begins: the time of a human life is a point. Its substance is always flowing. The senses are dim, the body decaying, the soul a whirl. Fortune is hard to read, and fame is without judgment. Everything of the body is a river; everything of the soul, a dream and smoke. Then comes the line in today's title. In Long's translation: "life is a warfare and a stranger's sojourn, and after-fame is oblivion." A war, because it's struggle. A stranger's sojourn, because we're travelers here, staying a while in a place that isn't ours to keep. Then the question: "What then is that which is able to conduct a man? One thing and only one, philosophy." For Marcus, philosophy wasn't a subject. It was a way of living: keeping the spirit within unharmed, above pleasure and pain; doing nothing without aim and nothing false; not depending on what others do or don't do; accepting what comes; and meeting death calmly, as nature's work. Listeners on this path will answer differently. Some are guided by a faith, some by a teacher, a text, a practice, a person. Marcus named his. The question is the gift: if life is a traveler's stay, what are you traveling by? So book two ends, and our week in it: stop spinning, mind your own mind, live ready to leave, see how fast things vanish, don't pry, don't wound yourself with anger. A long list of what slips away, and one thing to hold on to.
screen: `A POINT, A RIVER, A DREAM.` · `A WAR, AND A STRANGER'S STAY.` · `WHAT CAN GUIDE? PHILOSOPHY.` · `WHAT DO YOU TRAVEL BY?` · then, large: `A TRAVELER'S STAY.`

segments.voice: Picture yourself as a traveler in a borrowed room: your body, your days, your people, none of it yours to keep and all of it yours to care for. Ask quietly what guides you here, a faith, a teacher, a book, a practice, a person, a few hard-won rules, and name it. If you're not sure, that's honest too; sit with the question.
A stranger's sojourn. Marcus calls life a war and a traveler's stay, and asks what can guide us. For him, one thing: philosophy. Today's word.
Your line: a traveler's stay. A borrowed room, and a guide for the road. Rest well.
